source: Edwards, Coombs, Szyszka, Logishetty, Cobb (2021) Cognitive task analysis-based training in surgery: a meta-analysis
finding: Surgical trainees taught with CTA-designed material beat conventional training on procedural knowledge.
numbers: 12 studies kept from 2205 records (10 RCTs, 2 observational), 327 participants. Knowledge SMD 1.36 (95% CI 0.67 to 2.05), 4 studies, I2=60%. Random-effects model.
limits: Only 4 to 5 studies pooled. Small trials (mean 27 people). Mostly simulated tasks. Risk of bias rated some concern (no protocols, selective reporting).
agent_relevance: Lessons built from expert cue interviews can raise how well a learner (or a model reading them) knows a procedure. Moderate evidence, not proof.

source: Edwards et al. (2021) CTA meta-analysis, technical performance
finding: CTA-based training also raised hands-on performance, with the largest effect in true trainees.
numbers: Technical performance (global rating scores): trainees only SMD 2.06 (1.17 to 2.96), 4 studies, I2=61%. All 5 pooled studies: SMD 1.58 (0.31 to 2.85), P=0.010. With the medical-student study included, I2 was 87%.
limits: SMDs above 2 are implausibly large for education; likely inflated by small samples, publication bias, weak controls (for example a technical manual). No funnel plot reported.
agent_relevance: Do not copy the headline effect size into expectations for an LLM. Plan for effects much smaller than the surgical RCTs suggest.

source: Edwards et al. (2021) CTA meta-analysis, moderator: learner experience
finding: Benefit vanished for medical students. Both medical-student studies found no difference from conventional teaching on technical performance.
numbers: Bathalon 2005 (open cricothyrotomy) and Kowalewski 2017 (laparoscopic cholecystectomy, Touch Surgery app): no significant difference. Campbell 2011 also found equal cricothyrotomy performance. All trainee studies on technical performance were positive.
limits: Authors' explanation (learners need prior knowledge to use decision-point content) is a hypothesis, not tested. Student studies also differed in delivery and quality.
agent_relevance: Cue-based lessons seem to need a base-competent learner. A weak model may not gain from expert-decision lessons it cannot ground.

source: Edwards et al. (2021) CTA meta-analysis, method quality
finding: The CTA behind the training was often undocumented, and CTA content was confounded with delivery medium.
numbers: Only 7 of 12 studies described the CTA method; all 7 interviewed more than one expert; 3 used modified Delphi. 3 studies (Touch Surgery app) gave no detail on how content was derived. Controls ranged from a manual to courses. Shariff 2015 found no difference between a CTA study day and a CTA multimedia tool. MERSQI mean 13.6 (SD 1.35).
limits: Cannot separate CTA content from good multimedia plus structure. No dose-response or method comparison across studies.
agent_relevance: When we write lessons from interview data, test them against a plain-structure control, or we may only be measuring structure.

source: Sullivan, Yates, Inaba, Lam, Clark (2014) Use of CTA to reveal the instructional limitations of experts in teaching procedural skills. Acad Med
finding: Experts left out most of what a novice needs when they teach a procedure unprompted (abstract only was read).
numbers: 3 experts teaching cricothyrotomy vs a gold-standard task list built by 3 more surgeons. Omitted 71% (10/14) of clinical-knowledge steps, 51% (14/27) of action steps, 73% (3.6/5) of decision steps. How-to-do-it given for only 13% (3.6/27) of action steps.
limits: N=3 experts, one procedure, one lab. Gold standard built by the same method it validates, so partly circular.
agent_relevance: Free self-description by an expert, or a strong model, likely hides decision cues. Explicit probing passes are needed.

source: Sullivan et al. (2014) free recall versus prompted CTA recall
finding: Prompted CTA interview questions pulled out more knowledge than free recall (abstract only was read).
numbers: Steps described rose from 44% (20/46) in unprompted free recall to 66% (31/46) with CTA elicitation. Even prompted, about one third stayed missing.
limits: Same N=3 study. No test of whether the extra steps improved learner performance in this paper.
agent_relevance: Probing helps but does not finish the job; build a second pass (what-if, expert-novice contrast) into any lesson-extraction routine.

source: Clark, Pugh, Yates, Inaba, Green, Sullivan (2012) CTA to improve instructional descriptions of procedures. J Surg Res
finding: One CTA interview beat several free-recall interviews on completeness and accuracy (abstract only was read).
numbers: 10 trauma surgeons: 4 free recall, 5 free recall with simulation and instruments, 1 randomly chosen for CTA. CTA about 70% more complete and accurate. Unaided surgeons omitted nearly 70% of necessary decision steps. Simulation props helped free recall.
limits: The CTA arm is n=1, so the significance claim rests on one person. Nothing on learner outcomes.
agent_relevance: Props and concrete cases lift recall. For an agent, replay a concrete trace when asking why it chose an action.

source: Mansoori et al. (2025) Cognitive Task Analysis to Evaluate Resident Physician Decision Making in the ICU. ATS Scholar
finding: Critical decision method with a recognition-primed-decision template showed residents rely on volume heuristics and biases in septic-shock fluid decisions.
numbers: 11 of 23 eligible PGY-3 residents interviewed (48%), one hour each, median 7 days (IQR 6.5-11) after the case. 71 cues rated. Residents assumed more than 3-5 L meant no benefit from more fluid. 9 of 11 patients (82%) got guideline-concordant volume. All 11 named the 30 ml/kg rule.
limits: Single hospital, small N, retrospective self-report, no triangulation with observation, no outcome test. Authors call findings exploratory.
agent_relevance: Shows CDM yields concrete, checkable cue-and-heuristic lists, including wrong shortcuts. Good template for mining a model's own failure shortcuts.

source: Mansoori et al. (2025) reliability and saturation of CDM coding
finding: Coding of CDM data was moderately reliable and themes saturated early.
numbers: Fleiss kappa = 0.64 for cue-influence ratings (3 raters, 5-point scale, then consensus). Code saturation after interview 7, nothing new by interview 10. 4-person interview team, ATLAS.ti template coding.
limits: Kappa 0.64 is substantial but not high. Raters were also the interviewers, so not blind. No second site.
agent_relevance: About 7 to 10 cases per role looked enough to saturate themes here, a cheap budget for lesson mining. Expect noisy labels.

source: Cardiac arrest VR simulation with cued-recall CTA, expert vs novice team leaders (2025) Annals of Medicine
finding: Cued-recall CTA after a VR simulation separated experts from novices in reasoning style and strategy count.
numbers: 7 experts, 5 novices, 12 sessions of 10-15 min. 250 unique cognitive processes. Decision points 48 expert vs 45 novice; pitfalls 46 vs 33; strategies 77 vs 44; critical communications 23 vs 20. 86 subthemes (34.4%) unique to one group. Experts used inductive reasoning, novices deductive. Median cognitive load 53 (experts) vs 80 (novices).
limits: Convenience sample, one centre, groups differ in specialty (novices mostly family medicine). Experts may have known their team members. Novice critical-communication themes never saturated. Cognitive load self-rated.
agent_relevance: The expert-novice gap is largest in strategies and pitfalls, not in decision points. Lessons should store strategies and pitfalls, not only the decision list.

source: White et al. (2018) Getting inside the expert's head: eye-tracking aided CTA of trauma resuscitation. Ann Emerg Med
finding: Showing experts their own first-person eye-tracking video during CTA debrief surfaced unconscious cognition (abstract only was read).
numbers: 10 resuscitations, 4 expert team leaders, 18 months. All participants said the method uncovered previously unconscious cognition. 5 themes: logistic awareness, managing uncertainty, visual fixation, selective attention to information, anticipatory behaviors.
limits: N=4 experts. Self-report that the method helps is not a test of accuracy. No novice comparison.
agent_relevance: Replaying the real trace (here video, for us the action log) is a stronger probe than asking cold. Supports trace replay for agent self-review.

source: Hashimoto et al. (2019) Surgical procedural map scoring for decision-making in laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Am J Surg
finding: CTA interviews turned into procedural maps that distinguished attendings from residents (abstract only was read).
numbers: 6 attendings vs 6 residents. Operative steps 29.67 vs 23.3 (p=0.04). Crosslinks 3.2 vs 1.0 (p=0.005). Total map score 90.2 vs 63.2 (p=0.015). No difference in count of patient or surgeon factors.
limits: N=12. Maps built by researchers from interviews. Difference may be verbal fluency, not decision quality.
agent_relevance: Expert knowledge differs in links between steps (branches and cross-checks), not in number of factors. A lesson should encode links.

source: Hegde et al. (2020) Endoscopic submucosal dissection: a CTA framework toward training design. Surg Endosc
finding: Semi-structured CTA interviews of 4 experts and 4 novices plus 3 observations gave four categories: learning goals, challenges, strategies, decision-making (abstract only was read).
numbers: 8 interviewees, 3 observations. Purely qualitative; no effect size.
limits: No outcome test. Design-stage study only.
agent_relevance: Typical of the field: many cheap qualitative CTAs, very few that test the downstream lesson. Do not count them as effect evidence.

source: Riggle et al. (2014) Task analysis method for procedural training curriculum development. Perspect Med Educ
finding: A streamlined CTA for linear procedures needed fewer trained staff, fewer interviews and less expert time than full CTA (abstract only was read).
numbers: Central venous catheter insertion case. The abstract gives no numbers for time saved.
limits: Not compared head to head with full CTA on learning outcomes. Authors restrict the claim to linear procedures.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: heavy interview methods are justified for branching, uncertain tasks; for linear ones a cheap pass may do. Match effort to task type.

source: Wang, Zhang, Robinson, Loeb, Demszky (2024) Bridging the Novice-Expert Gap via Models of Decision-Making (arXiv 2310.10648v3)
finding: Using a CTA-derived expert decision model (student error, strategy, intention) in the prompt made GPT-4 tutor responses much better.
numbers: 700 real tutoring conversations (train 420, val 70, test 210), 120 topics, two expert responses each. Teachers judged 40 pairs per model, 3 blind raters each. GPT-4 overall score: expert decisions 0.83 vs none 0.51; preference 0.95 vs 0.54. Abstract: +76% more preferred. Llama-2 overall 0.49 vs 0.53 (no gain); GPT-3.5 0.45 vs 0.28. Human expert reference 1.02.
limits: Pairwise scores on 40 pairs per model; one domain (math tutoring); Prolific teachers as raters, not learning outcomes. The expert-decision arm uses gold labels on the test items.
agent_relevance: Best direct LLM test of a CTA-to-prompt route. Gain depends on model strength: Llama-2 gained nothing overall and GPT-3.5 little, so a decision scaffold needs a capable model.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Bridge: random and self-generated decisions
finding: Decision content matters. Random decisions hurt; the model's own decisions helped GPT-4 as much as expert ones, but gave less varied paths.
numbers: GPT-4 overall: expert 0.83, self 0.84, random 0.26, none 0.51. Abstract: random decisions cut GPT-4 quality by 97% relative to expert decisions. Self decisions with GPT-3.5 scored 0.16 (worse than none, 0.28). Expert decision paths were diverse; LLM paths were not (lower entropy), read by the authors as homogenization.
limits: Same small human evaluation. Self success may reflect GPT-4 already holding the pedagogy. Significance not shown for every pair.
agent_relevance: For a strong model, the decide-then-respond structure may carry most of the gain; expert data may add diversity more than quality. Test self-elicited versus expert-elicited lessons.

source: Wang, Ribeiro, Robinson, Loeb, Demszky (2024, rev. 2026) Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise (arXiv 2410.03017)
finding: A randomized field trial of an LLM tool built on the Bridge expert-decision method raised student mastery.
numbers: 900 tutors, 1,800 students (abstract); preregistered; intent-to-treat +4 percentage points mastery (p<0.01); +9 pp for lower-rated tutors; about $20 per tutor per year. Abstract says over 550,000 messages classified; the PDF text says 350,000 and 1,013 analysed students, so counts differ between versions.
limits: Under-served, mostly Hispanic grade 3-6 sample in one district. Authors say the effect may be smaller for experienced tutors. Tutors flagged unsuitable grade-level suggestions. Outcome is lesson mastery, not end-of-year tests.
agent_relevance: Strongest real-world test of expert-decision scaffolding. Gains are biggest for the weakest performers, matching the novice-benefit pattern in the surgery meta-analysis.

source: Du, Jiang, Shen, Ren (2019) Eliciting Knowledge from Experts: Automatic Transcript Parsing for CTA (arXiv 1906.11384)
finding: Early machine parsing of CTA interview transcripts into structured action knowledge worked only modestly.
numbers: Mention-level F1 on span extraction: rule baseline 18.6, CRF 38.1, LSTM-CRF 35.6. Weakly supervised, small labelled set.
limits: Pre-LLM models (GloVe, BERT features, LSTM-CRF). Not a test of whether parsed knowledge improves performance.
agent_relevance: Shows human coding labour was the CTA bottleneck. LLMs now do this step, but I found no opened study measuring their accuracy at it.

source: Stanik, Puhlfurss, Mahler, Sasu, Reip, Maalej (2022) Lessons learned from customizing and applying ACTA for emergency medical care (arXiv 2108.05622)
finding: A digital, shortened applied CTA (ACTA) workshop was workable but narrowed scope.
numbers: Digital workshop 6 hours; participants made 34 screen sketches; two thirds would have preferred on-site; none wanted asynchronous take-home tasks. A second workshop ran two days of about 8 hours each.
limits: Requirements-engineering case, not a performance test. Small N.
agent_relevance: Time-limited CTA drops rare features and edge cases; sketches covered near-ideal use. Expect edge cases to be what is lost when lessons are mined quickly.

source: Review: A Multi-Disciplinary Review of Knowledge Acquisition Methods (arXiv 1802.09669, 2018)
finding: Review places the Critical Decision Method among human-agent elicitation methods: time consuming, needs an elicitor with domain expertise, uses multi-pass retrospection.
numbers: Classifies methods into human, human-inspired and autonomous-agent groups. A table rates CDM as rich output (read from imperfect extracted table text).
limits: Descriptive review; no comparative effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Cost and elicitor skill are the known costs of CDM; an LLM elicitor changes exactly those two terms.

source: Irons et al. (2024) Towards a criteria-based approach to selecting human-AI interaction mode (arXiv 2411.07406)
finding: CTA outputs (decision points, challenges, expert strategies) from three science tasks were used to score whether AI should automate, augment or collaborate.
numbers: Three tasks: genome annotation, biological collections curation, protein crystallization. Scoring rubric built; preliminary application only; no performance data.
limits: Not an outcome study.
agent_relevance: CTA decision-point lists can feed a routing rule (when to act alone, when to ask). Idea only; unvalidated.

source: Klein, Calderwood, MacGregor (1989) Critical decision method for eliciting knowledge. IEEE Trans SMC 19(3)
finding: Founding paper of the Critical Decision Method: incident-based, multi-sweep retrospective interviews with probes. Not opened this session; seen only as a citation.
numbers: Not read; no figures recorded.
limits: Not verified. Known critique: single-informant retrospective reports.
agent_relevance: The method skeleton (incident, timeline, decision points, probes, what-if) is the part to borrow.

source: Tofel-Grehl & Feldon (2013) Cognitive task analysis-based training: a meta-analysis of studies. J Cogn Eng Decis Making 7(3)
finding: Earlier meta-analysis of CTA-based training, cited by Edwards 2021. Publisher page returned 403, so not opened and no numbers recorded.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not verified.
agent_relevance: Open later to get the pooled effect size and moderators.

source: Nisbett & Wilson (1977) Telling more than we can know: verbal reports on mental processes
finding: Classic challenge to the accuracy of introspective reports of why people act as they do. Not opened.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not verified here.
agent_relevance: Boundary on every interview method: stated reasons may be reconstructions. Sullivan 2014 shows omission; this line is about distortion.

source: Ericsson & Simon (1993) Protocol Analysis: verbal reports as data
finding: Held view: concurrent think-aloud is generally valid; retrospective reports less so unless close in time and well cued. Not opened.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not verified here.
agent_relevance: Supports short delay and concrete cues, as in Mansoori's 7-day median gap. Check against the protocol-analysis subfield file.
